transcript.content: Hello, thank you for coming in today. What brings you to the clinic?

Well, I... I suppose I'm here because of work. I'm a cashier, you see, over at the grocery store, and lately things have been—well, they haven't been going smoothly. I've been there a long time, and I know how to do the job, but recently, I just... I get stuck. It’s hard to explain. I’ll be ringing someone up, and suddenly I have to tap the scanner. Not just once, but in a specific pattern, over and over, even though it doesn't do anything to ring up the groceries. Or, or I'll go to give them their change, and my hand will just freeze right over the cash drawer. I’ll just stand there, holding my hand out, and I can't seem to make it move to grab the bills. And the customer is just standing there staring at me, waiting for their money, and I know they're waiting, but I just can't seem to unfreeze. It’s like my body is doing things that don’t make any sense for what I’m supposed to be doing right then. And, well, it’s causing problems. Last week, it happened during a rush, and the line got so backed up, and the manager came over, and... well, I got written up for it. I've never been written up before. I have a bachelor's degree, you know, I shouldn't be having trouble working a cash register, but I just keep getting caught in these... these actions that don't fit what's happening around me.
When you find yourself tapping in that specific pattern or freezing, is there a particular thought or worry running through your mind that drives you to do it?

Well, that's the thing that's so confusing to me, and frankly, it's what makes the whole situation so incredibly frustrating. You'd think there would be a reason, right? Like maybe I'm worried the register will break, or I'm counting the items in my head, or I'm afraid of making a mistake with the change... but no. No, not at all. There isn't a worry or a specific thought like that driving it. 

When I'm tapping the scanner—and it's usually the side of the scanner, right where the little red laser comes out, I always seem to tap it with my knuckles, never my fingertips, which is strange in itself—my mind is just... well, it's not worried about anything. It's almost empty, or maybe just disconnected from the action. And when I freeze over the cash drawer, it's the exact same thing. 

Like last Tuesday, when my manager, Greg, came over. He's a nice enough guy, usually, a lot younger than me, maybe 30 or 32, but he was really stressed because it was senior discount day and the lines were backed up all the way down the frozen food aisle. He came up and asked me what I was thinking about, why I was just standing there like a statue with a ten-dollar bill hovering in my hand. And I tried to tell him, I really did try to explain, but there just wasn't anything running through my head. I wasn't daydreaming about my evening or worrying about paying my own rent or thinking the customer was going to yell at me. I just... the movement simply stops. Or the tapping just happens. 

There's no fear that something terrible will happen if I don't tap the plastic, no grand plan behind it. It's just my body doing these things, and my brain is just sort of sitting there, watching it happen, without any particular thoughts or worries attached to it at all. It's baffling, because with a bachelor's degree, I feel like I should be able to sit down, analyze the situation, and figure out the psychological root cause of why I'm doing this, but when I look for a reason or a thought... there's just nothing there to find.
Have you ever heard voices, sounds, or noises that other people couldn't hear?

Well, yes, actually... I have. And I'm glad you asked that, because it's been another thing that's been making work so difficult lately. It happens most days now, really. I'll be standing there at the register—register number four, usually, that's my assigned lane because it's closest to the door and I like the natural light—and I'll hear... well, it sounds exactly like a couple of people talking, just off to the side of me. 

At first, I thought it was just customers, you know, whispering about me or maybe chatting in the next lane. But the things they say... sometimes they'll call my name, just clear as day, coming from the direction of the stockroom. 'Hey, David,' or whatever, just like that. And I'll turn around, fully expecting to see Greg or one of the stock boys needing me to do a price check or help unload a pallet, but... there's nobody there. The stockroom doors will be completely shut. 

Other times, right in the middle of a transaction, I'll hear these voices saying I rang something up wrong. They'll say, 'He scanned that twice,' or 'He missed the barcode on the cereal.' And I'll stop—which probably doesn't help with the freezing thing I mentioned earlier—and I'll check the screen, and I'll ask the customer, 'Did you say something about the cereal?' And they just look at me like I'm crazy. They didn't hear a thing. The bagger didn't hear a thing. 

It's so vivid, Doctor. It's not like a thought in my head, it's a sound in the air, bouncing off the linoleum floors and the metal shelves. I've even gone so far as to walk down the aisle a bit, thinking maybe someone dropped their Bluetooth earpiece or there's a radio left on somewhere, but I never find anything. It's just... these voices, talking about what I'm doing, or calling for me, and I'm the only one who seems to be able to pick up the frequency. It's terribly distracting when you're trying to count out exact change for a twenty-dollar bill and someone who isn't there is telling you that you've already messed it up.

Medical conditions? Like, physical illnesses and that sort of thing? No, no, actually, my physical health is... well, it's remarkably good, all things considered. I mean, I see my primary care doctor, Dr. Aris, over at the clinic on 4th Street—I've been going to him for, oh, it must be twelve years now, ever since my previous doctor retired and moved down to Arizona—and Dr. Aris always tells me I'm in great shape for a man my age. I'm 54, you know, and you look around at other guys in their fifties and they're on all sorts of pills for blood pressure, or diabetes, or they have bad knees or bad backs, but... but not me. 

I don't have any neurological problems or diseases or anything like that at all. I try to take really good care of myself. I walk to the grocery store for my shifts, which is a good mile and a half each way, and I do that rain or shine. Well, unless it's really pouring or snowing heavily, then I might catch the 42 bus, but usually I walk. My heart is strong, my blood work from my last physical back in October was completely normal... Dr. Aris even said my cholesterol went down a few points because I made a concerted effort to switch from having eggs and sausage to just a bowl of plain oatmeal with a handful of blueberries every morning. It's not nearly as satisfying of a breakfast, I'll admit, but it does the trick for the cholesterol. 

I did hit my head once, years and years ago when I was getting my bachelor's degree—I slipped on some wet leaves right outside the science building on my way to a seminar—but the campus nurse checked me out and I didn't even have a concussion, just a little bump on the back of my skull that went away in a few days. So, no, there's absolutely nothing wrong with my body physically, no seizures or strokes or whatever else might cause a person's brain to misfire. It's just... it's just this bizarre freezing up with my hands and the tapping and those voices at the register. But physically? Physically, I'm fit as a fiddle.

Do you ever feel like people are watching you, spying on you, or deliberately trying to harm you?

No, no, I wouldn't say that at all. I mean... who would want to spy on me? I live a very, very quiet life, Doctor. I've been in the same little duplex over on Elm Street for going on fifteen years now—ever since the management company raised the rent at my old apartment over near the university campus—and my neighbors are all just older retired folks or young couples who keep entirely to themselves. Mrs. Higgins next door might peek out her blinds sometimes when the mail carrier comes, but she's just waiting for her catalog deliveries, she's certainly not spying on me. 

And as for people trying to harm me... no, I don't have any enemies. I don't owe anybody money, I don't have any angry ex-wives—I never actually married, just never seemed to find the right time after I finished my bachelor's degree, what with getting settled into working and all. At the grocery store, sure, people look at me, but that's just because I'm the cashier. They're looking at my name tag, or they're watching the little monitor to make sure the sale prices ring up correctly—you know how people get if a coupon doesn't scan right away, they want to make sure they aren't being overcharged. But they aren't watching me with any sort of malicious intent. 

Nobody is following me on my walk to work, nobody is tapping my phone or anything like you see in those espionage movies or read about in those thriller novels. It's really just... well, it's just those voices I mentioned earlier, the ones at register four. And even they aren't threatening to hurt me or anything like that, they're just terribly critical about how I scan the items or count the change. But actual, real people trying to plot against me or do me harm? No, no, I've never felt anything like that at all. My life is quite ordinary in that regard.
